title: Go to the ant (Proverbs 6:6–11)
hookLine: the ant has no boss, yet stores food in summer
carry: a little folding of the hands

lines: A LINE OF ANTS ON A HILLSIDE.
cards: Late summer, on a dry hillside in the land of Israel. On the path, a line of ants, each carrying a seed bigger than its head. Down a hole they go, up they come empty, and back out to the grass for another.
Below ground, chambers packed with grain, stored against the winter. Nobody is shouting orders. No ant stands at the top with a clipboard.
They just work, in the season for working. Someone in ancient Israel crouched down and watched this for a long time, and wrote it up as a lesson for a person still in bed.

teach.b: Proverbs chapter six, in the King James Bible: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest."
A sluggard is someone who keeps putting things off, and the teacher here is tiny. No guide, overseer, or ruler: that's sharp observation.
Biologists say an ant colony does have a queen, but she lays eggs; she doesn't give orders. The work gets done without a boss.
And the seed-storing is real too: in that region, harvester ants carry seeds underground and keep them in granaries.

teach.h: A LITTLE SLEEP, A LITTLE SLUMBER
teach.b: Then the teacher turns to the person in bed: "How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep." Hear the rhythm.
It's not one huge decision to be lazy. It's a little more. Five more minutes.
Snooze. And then: "So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man." Not slowly.
Like a traveler at the door, like a robber. Two cautions, because Proverbs isn't a boot camp.

teach.h: WORK IN SEASON, REST IN SEASON
teach.b: The same Bible commands a day of rest every week, and the ant works in its season, not every hour.

teach.h: GO TO THE ANT, THOU SLUGGARD; CONSIDER HER WAYS.
teach.b: And elsewhere Proverbs suggests the poor can lose their harvest to injustice, not idleness. This saying is about one thing: the small, repeated delay. The ant doesn't wait to be told.
It sees the season, and it moves.

how: Christians often teach Proverbs 6:6–11 to children and young people as a lesson in diligence, alongside the weekly Sabbath or Lord's Day rest that keeps work in its place.

games.q: it's summer. food is everywhere. no boss is watching. you're an ant. what do you do?
o: wait for someone to tell you what to do.
games.why: "which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, provideth her meat in the summer." the ant moves in the season, without being told.

practice: Picture one small thing you've been putting off, a dish in the sink, a one-line email, a bill, a drawer, and see yourself doing it start to finish, with no boss telling you to.
Notice the moment you'd usually say, just a little later. If you pray, ask for help with the next small thing; if not, simply let the picture be clear.

wordCard.voice: Sluggard. Proverbs' name for the person who keeps putting things off, sent to watch an ant with no boss working all summer.

orig.note: Hebrew: ant. it appears only twice in the Bible, both times in Proverbs.

carryVoice: Your line: a little folding of the hands. It's never one big decision, just a little more. See you tomorrow.
